props.title: La Luna
props.initialSlug: Aristocrat's erotic journey through decadent Rome

sections.content: Bertolucci's erotic drama La Luna stands as one of cinema's most daring explorations of an incestuous mother-son relationship, following in the provocative footsteps of Louis Malle's Murmur of the Heart (1971). Jill Clayburgh delivers a fearless performance as an American opera singer whose relationship with her teenage son becomes disturbingly intimate as she tries to help him overcome heroin addiction. The film's striking imagery - particularly the scenes of Rome bathed in golden light - showcases Vittorio Storaro's masterful cinematography, while Ennio Morricone's score weaves opera and contemporary music to underscore the psychological complexity.

sections.content: La Luna marked a significant shift in Bertolucci's career, coming after his political epics 1900 (1976) and The Conformist (1970). The film's explicit handling of taboo themes aligns it with other boundary-pushing works of the era like Pasolini's Salò (1975), though Bertolucci opts for a more lyrical, psychoanalytic approach. The film's operatic framework - with references to Mozart's "The Magic Flute" and the myth of the Moon Goddess - elevates the material beyond mere shock value.

The film's influence can be traced through later works dealing with complex maternal relationships, from Pedro Almodóvar's All About My Mother (1999) to Darren Aronofsky's Black Swan (2010). Its bold mixing of high culture (opera) with transgressive themes paved the way for directors like Peter Greenaway, particularly in films like The Cook, the Thief, His Wife & Her Lover (1989). sections.content: Bertolucci's use of opera as both backdrop and metaphor in La Luna creates a fascinating dialogue with other films that employ classical music to explore psychological extremes, such as Werner Herzog's Fitzcarraldo (1982) and James Ivory's The Wild Party (1975). The film's Rome locations, captured with Storaro's characteristic attention to natural light, create a mythic atmosphere that contrasts sharply with the contemporary drug culture storyline.
